structured.recommendation: Adopt a progressive/canary rollout policy with automated health-gated promotion. Ship every change through a small canary slice first, watch risk signals, and auto-promote to the full fleet when gates pass or auto-roll-back when they fail. This directly serves the goal of reducing deployment risk (issue:L1) by limiting blast radius to a subset before full exposure, while preserving delivery speed (issue:L2) because changes still flow continuously and promotion is automated rather than gated on manual sign-off. This is my recommended answer to the rollout-policy question (issue:L3): canary + automatic gates is the policy that balances both constraints better than either an all-at-once push (fast but risky) or a slow manual staged rollout (safe but slow).

evidence.claim: The stated goal is to reduce deployment risk, which canary rollouts serve by limiting blast radius.
Delivery speed must be preserved, which automated gate-based promotion maintains by avoiding manual bottlenecks.
The question asks which rollout policy balances risk and speed, which the alternative answers.

assumptions.statement: The system has health/risk telemetry (error rate, latency, saturation) fast enough to gate canary promotion.
assumptions.if_false_then: Automated gates cannot function, so canary degrades to timed staged rollout and the speed benefit shrinks.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Confirm observability signals and their detection latency exist for the deployed service.

assumptions.statement: Traffic or fleet can be split into a small canary slice.
assumptions.if_false_then: Canary is infeasible; a blue-green or feature-flag approach would be the fallback.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Check whether the routing/deploy layer supports partial rollout.

risks: If risk signals are noisy, auto-rollback may cause flapping and slow effective delivery.
Canary tooling adds operational complexity that a small team may not sustain.
Low-traffic services may not accumulate enough canary signal to gate confidently, weakening the risk reduction.
what_would_change_my_view: Evidence that deployments are rare/large-batch, where blue-green with instant switch may balance better than canary.
Absence of usable real-time telemetry, favoring a manual staged rollout instead.
A stated constraint that changes must reach 100% simultaneously (e.g., schema/protocol coupling).
structured.next_action: Confirm the two load-bearing assumptions (telemetry latency and traffic-splittability), then define concrete promotion gates and rollback thresholds for the canary policy.
